parts.title: Ordering made-to-measure curtains
parts.context: A customer phones a shop to order curtains for a bay window.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a customer phoning a shop to order made-to-measure curtains. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Hartwell Home Furnishings, Gareth speaking.

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: Hello. I'd like to order some curtains, please. They're for my living room, and I want them made to measure.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Certainly. I'll take your details first, and then we can talk about fabrics.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The curtains are for the living room, so 'living room' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: It's Priyanka Fernandes. That's F-E-R-N-A-N-D-E-S.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Thank you, Ms Fernandes. How many windows are the curtains for?

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: Three. It's a bay window, so there are three separate sections, and I'd like a matching pair for the middle one.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: And have you thought about the fabric?

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: I liked the velvet, but I think it's too heavy for a bay window. I'll choose linen.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: A good choice. And the colour?

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: I thought of blue to begin with, but the walls are already blue, so I'll go for grey.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: That will look elegant. Would you like a lining?

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: Yes, a blackout lining, please, because the street light shines straight into the room.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Now, how will the curtains hang? We can fit them to a metal track, or to a pole.

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: I'd prefer a wooden pole, I think. It looks more traditional, and it suits the room.

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: Fine. Made-to-measure curtains normally take four weeks, but at the moment we're very busy, so it will be six.

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: That's all right. I'm not in a hurry. How much will it all be?

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: We'll give you the full price when the fitter has measured your windows. For now, we ask for a deposit of fifty pounds, to start the order.

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: No problem. And is fitting included?

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: No, the fitting is charged separately, and it's forty pounds for a bay window. Our fitter will measure first, and fit the curtains when they are ready.

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: And when do I pay the balance?

script.speaker: gareth
script.text: On delivery, when the fitter brings the curtains. We accept cards, but not cheques.

script.speaker: priyanka
script.text: Lovely. Thank you for your help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A tour of a castle's gardens
parts.context: The head gardener introduces the gardens of a castle.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the head gardener of a castle giving visitors a tour of the gardens. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the gardens of Hartwell Castle. I'm Joan Rowe, the head gardener. Please look at the map. We're at the entrance, at the bottom, and the castle is at the top, at the end of the main path.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: Just inside the entrance, on the left of the path, is the tearoom. I'd keep that for the end of the tour, as the scones are excellent.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: Walking up the main path, on the left at the bottom is the greenhouse, which is where we grow most of our plants. Above it, in the middle on the left, is the maze, and at the top, beside the castle, the herb garden.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: On the right, opposite the greenhouse, is the pond, with its fountain. Above the pond, in the middle on the right, you'll find the orchard. And the rose garden is beside the castle, at the top on the right, though the roses are only at their best in June.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: A little history. People often assume that the gardens were designed by a famous landscape architect, but they weren't. They were created in eighteen ninety by the owner of the castle, Lady Margaret, who was a keen gardener, and she planned every bed herself.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: The maze was her favourite. It has more than a thousand trees, planted in tight rows, and it takes about twenty minutes to find your way to the middle. Some visitors need much longer, but the fastest time on record is four minutes.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: In the orchard we grow forty varieties of apple. We don't make cider, as some visitors expect. The fruit is used in the tearoom and sold in the shop, and in autumn you can buy it straight from the trees.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: The greenhouse isn't a place for exotic fruit. Most of our plants are grown there from seed, and then moved out to fill the flower beds each spring, so it's a busy place, and you're welcome to look in.

script.speaker: rowe
script.text: And on Sundays at two o'clock we offer a free guided walk, which lasts about an hour, and is very popular. Please do join us, and don't pick the flowers. Now, shall we begin?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A case study on fair-trade coffee
parts.context: Two economics students plan a case study of a coffee cooperative.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two economics students, Priti and Sam, discussing a case study on fair-trade coffee. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: priti
script.text: Sam, for our economics assignment on fair-trade coffee, I've chosen a cooperative in Peru as the case study.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Why Peru and not Ethiopia? Ethiopia is the original home of coffee.

script.speaker: priti
script.text: True, but there's much more published data about Peruvian cooperatives, and the one I chose has an annual report in English.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: That makes sense. What's the main argument? That fair trade is good for farmers?

script.speaker: priti
script.text: More carefully than that. I want to argue that it helps, but the benefits are limited, because only some of the extra price reaches the farmer.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: How did the cooperative start?

script.speaker: priti
script.text: In nineteen ninety-four, with about forty farmers. Now it has more than five thousand members.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: What's the biggest benefit the farmers mention?

script.speaker: priti
script.text: I thought it would be the higher price, but in the interviews they mostly mentioned training. For example, they learned how to grow coffee without chemicals.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: And what are the criticisms?

script.speaker: priti
script.text: The main one is that certification fees are too high for the smallest farms, so the poorest farmers can't afford to join.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: Let's describe the supply chain. Start with the growers.

script.speaker: priti
script.text: They receive a guaranteed minimum price, whatever happens to the world market. That's the central idea of fair trade.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: The cooperative?

script.speaker: priti
script.text: It pays for training for its members, as well as a school fund, using the extra money, called the premium.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: The exporters?

script.speaker: priti
script.text: They face rising costs, mainly because of shipping and fuel, and they say their margins are shrinking.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: The roasters?

script.speaker: priti
script.text: Small roasters are expanding quickly, because customers want fair-trade coffee that's fresh.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: And finally, the supermarkets.

script.speaker: priti
script.text: They take the largest share of the profit. That's the surprising figure in the data, about half of the final price.

script.speaker: sam
script.text: That should make a strong conclusion. I'll draw a diagram of the chain.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the Maya
parts.context: A history lecture on the Maya civilisation and its decline.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the Maya civilisation. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we're looking at the Maya, one of the most advanced civilisations of the ancient Americas. They lived in what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala and Belize, and their classic period lasted from about the year two hundred and fifty to nine hundred.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The Maya were not a single empire. They were a collection of city-states, each ruled by a king, and often at war with one another. The largest cities, such as Tikal, may have had more than fifty thousand inhabitants.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: They built impressive stone pyramids, and they did it without metal tools, and without wheeled vehicles or animals to carry loads. Many of their cities had no rivers nearby, so farmers collected rainwater in huge reservoirs, and grew maize, beans and squash.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The Maya also developed the most fully developed written language in the ancient Americas. Their hieroglyphs were carved on stone monuments called stelae, and recorded the deeds of kings and the dates of battles. It took scholars much of the twentieth century to decode them.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: They were brilliant mathematicians. Their number system was based on twenty, not ten, and they had a symbol for zero, which was a great achievement, since many other civilisations never developed one. They also tracked the movements of the sun, the moon and Venus, and predicted eclipses with great accuracy.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Cacao beans were so valuable that they were used as money, as well as being made into a bitter drink for the elite.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Around the year nine hundred, many of the cities in the south were abandoned. Historians used to blame a single cause, but now the evidence points to several: warfare, overpopulation, and above all, a series of long droughts, which ruined the harvests. Yet the Maya did not disappear. About six million Maya people live in the region today, and many still speak Mayan languages.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: New technology is changing what we know. In two thousand and eighteen, researchers used laser scanning from aircraft to see through the trees, and found tens of thousands of previously unknown buildings hidden under the forest in Guatemala. There is clearly much more to learn. Next week we'll look at the Aztecs.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
